name: Upgrade plan, drain & schedule diagnosis
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration (25%). Drill EVERY node-level kubeadm corner harder than the exam: inspect component versions, read the kubelet config and static-pod manifests, mint a worker join token, perform the drain/uncordon maintenance dance, renew control-plane certificates, read an upgrade plan, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. All graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state.

questions.title: Drain then uncordon a node
questions.teach:
For node maintenance you `drain` (cordon + evict pods), do the work, then `uncordon` to let the scheduler use the node again: `kubectl drain <node>`, then `kubectl uncordon <node>`.

**Gotcha:** plain `drain` errors on real nodes — you need `--ignore-daemonsets`, plus `--force` to evict a bare (unmanaged) pod and `--delete-emptydir-data` if a pod uses emptyDir.
questions.prompt:
A bare Pod `drain-me` is pinned to worker $W2. Drain $W2 (evicting the workload), then uncordon it when "maintenance" is done.

Target: $W2 ends `schedulable` (`.spec.unschedulable` unset) AND no running `drain-me` pod remains on $W2.
questions.hint: `kubectl drain "$W2" --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force`, confirm with `kubectl get pods -o wide`, then `kubectl uncordon "$W2"`.
questions.solution:
kubectl drain "$W2" --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl uncordon "$W2"
kubectl get node "$W2"

verification.description: $W2 is schedulable and holds no running drain-me pod

questions.eli5:
Picture a node as a hotel floor full of guests (pods), and you need to do maintenance — fix the plumbing, say. You can't work with guests still in the rooms, and you don't want the front desk sending *new* guests up while you work.

**Draining** does both in one move: `kubectl drain <node>`

- First it **cordons** the floor — hangs a "no new check-ins" sign so the scheduler stops placing pods here.
- Then it **evicts** the current guests, politely moving them to other floors (other nodes).

When the plumbing's fixed, you **uncordon**: `kubectl uncordon <node>` takes the sign down so the front desk can use the floor again.

The complication: real floors always have a few permanent staff you *can't* evict (DaemonSet pods like the network agent and log collector) and sometimes an oddball guest with no booking record (a bare pod) or one storing stuff in a scratch drawer (emptyDir). Plain `drain` refuses and errors until you tell it how to handle these.

**Watch out for:**

- **Plain `drain` errors on real nodes.** You almost always need `--ignore-daemonsets`. Add `--force` to evict a bare (unmanaged) pod, and `--delete-emptydir-data` if a pod uses emptyDir (that data is lost — that's the point of the flag).
- **Drain only evicts; it doesn't delete the node.** The node stays, just unschedulable.
- **Don't forget to uncordon.** A drained node stays `SchedulingDisabled` forever until you uncordon it — a classic "why won't anything schedule here" trap.
- `cordon` alone just blocks new pods; `drain` = cordon **plus** evict.
questions.deepDive:
## Node maintenance: cordon, drain & uncordon — full rundown

### Mental model
Taking a node out of service safely is a three-beat dance:
1. **cordon** — mark the node `unschedulable` so no *new* pods land (existing pods keep running).
2. **drain** — cordon **and** evict the existing pods so the node is empty.
3. **uncordon** — clear the `unschedulable` flag so the scheduler can use the node again.

`drain` uses the **Eviction API**, so it respects **PodDisruptionBudgets** (PDBs) — it won't evict faster than a PDB allows.

### The commands
```bash
kubectl cordon   <node>        # block new pods only (sets .spec.unschedulable=true)
kubectl drain    <node> [flags]# cordon + evict existing pods
kubectl uncordon <node>        # unset .spec.unschedulable
```
State check:
```bash
kubectl get nodes                          # STATUS shows "Ready,SchedulingDisabled"
kubectl get node <node> -o jsonpath='{.spec.unschedulable}'; echo   # true / empty
```

### Why plain `drain` fails, and the flags that fix it
| Flag | When you need it | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--ignore-daemonsets` | always on real nodes | skips DaemonSet pods (they can't be evicted/rescheduled elsewhere) |
| `--force` | a **bare** pod (not owned by a controller) exists | deletes the orphan pod outright (it won't be recreated) |
| `--delete-emptydir-data` | a pod uses an `emptyDir` volume | permits eviction, **acknowledging that emptyDir data is lost** |
| `--grace-period=<s>` | override pod terminationGracePeriod | shutdown grace window |
| `--timeout=<dur>` | cap how long drain waits | gives up after the duration |
| `--pod-selector` / `--disable-eviction` | advanced | filter pods / bypass the eviction API (ignores PDBs — dangerous) |

A typical real-world drain:
```bash
kubectl drain "$W2" --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
```

### What drain does and does NOT touch
| Pod kind | Drained? |
|---|---|
| Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet pod | ✅ evicted, rescheduled elsewhere |
| DaemonSet pod | ⏭️ skipped (with `--ignore-daemonsets`) |
| Bare (unmanaged) pod | needs `--force`; **gone for good** |
| Mirror (static) pod | never evicted — managed by kubelet on the node |

Drain does **not** delete the node object or stop the kubelet; the node simply stays `SchedulingDisabled` and empty.

### Fit in the upgrade flow
During a `kubeadm` node upgrade:
```bash
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets          # move workloads off
# upgrade kubeadm, run: kubeadm upgrade node
# upgrade kubelet + kubectl packages, restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon <node>                           # back in service
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Plain `drain` errors** — "cannot delete DaemonSet-managed Pods" / "pods not managed by ...". Add `--ignore-daemonsets` and usually `--force`/`--delete-emptydir-data`.
- **Forgetting `uncordon`** leaves the node `SchedulingDisabled` — pods pinned there sit `Pending`. This is a classic diagnosis trap.
- `cordon` ≠ `drain`: cordon only blocks new pods; drain also evicts.
- `--delete-emptydir-data` **destroys** that pod's emptyDir data — expected, but know it.
- Drain honours **PDBs** and may block; `--disable-eviction` bypasses them (last resort).
- A node can be `Ready,SchedulingDisabled` — "Ready" doesn't mean "schedulable".

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl drain "$W2" --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
kubectl get nodes                      # confirm SchedulingDisabled + pods gone
# ...maintenance...
kubectl uncordon "$W2"                  # re-enable scheduling
```

questions.title: Read a kubeadm upgrade plan
questions.teach:
`kubeadm upgrade plan` is a READ-ONLY report: it lists which versions you can upgrade to and the components it would bump. You run it before `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X.Y`. The plan reasons about the running server (apiserver) version, which `kubectl version` reports.

**Gotcha:** the old `kubectl version --short` flag was removed — read the server line from plain `kubectl version`, or pull just the string with `kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion`.
questions.prompt:
On $CP, run `kubeadm upgrade plan` to read it. To prove the control plane is healthy and reporting a version, write the server (apiserver) version string to `/tmp/serverversion.txt` on $CP.

Target: `/tmp/serverversion.txt` on $CP contains a `v<major>.<minor>.<patch>` Kubernetes version.
questions.hint: Read it the easy way from your terminal: `kubectl version` and look at the **Server Version** line. To capture just that string and write the file on $CP: `V=$(kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion)` then `docker exec "$CP" sh -c "echo $V > /tmp/serverversion.txt"`.
questions.solution:
# read the plan (exam: this is what you run before `kubeadm upgrade apply`)
docker exec "$CP" kubeadm upgrade plan

# read the server version — plain and simple
kubectl version                       # look at the "Server Version: v1.X.Y" line

# capture just that string into the file on $CP
V=$(kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion)
docker exec "$CP" sh -c "echo $V > /tmp/serverversion.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/serverversion.txt
questions.eli5:
Before you renovate a house, a good builder walks through with a clipboard and writes up a plan: "here's what you've got now, here's the next version you could move to, and here's every fixture I'd have to swap." They don't touch a hammer yet — it's just a report you read and approve.

`kubeadm upgrade plan` is exactly that clipboard. It's **read-only**. It looks at your running cluster, tells you which newer versions you're eligible to upgrade to, and lists the components it would bump (apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler, kube-proxy, CoreDNS). You run it *before* the real command, `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X.Y`, which is the one that actually swings the hammer.

To figure out the plan, kubeadm needs to know what version the cluster is *running now*. That's the **Server Version** — the version of the API server — which you can read yourself with `kubectl version`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`kubeadm upgrade plan` changes nothing.** It only reads and reports. The destructive one is `kubeadm upgrade apply`.
- **The `kubectl version --short` flag was removed.** Don't rely on it. Use plain `kubectl version` and read the "Server Version" line, or grab just the string with `kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion`.
- **"Client Version" ≠ "Server Version".** The client is your kubectl; the server is the cluster's API server. The plan cares about the *server*.
- You can only upgrade **one minor version at a time** (e.g. 1.30 → 1.31, never 1.30 → 1.32). The plan enforces this.
- Upgrade the **control plane first**, then workers; and `kubeadm` the binary before `kubeadm upgrade apply`.
questions.deepDive:
## Reading a kubeadm upgrade plan & the version string — full rundown

### Mental model
`kubeadm upgrade plan` is a **read-only** report: it inspects the running control plane, checks which target versions are available, and lists the components it would bump. Nothing changes until you run the imperative `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X.Y`. The plan reasons about the **running apiserver version**, which `kubectl version` reports as *Server Version*.

### The read-only plan
```bash
kubeadm upgrade plan              # report only — safe to run anytime
kubeadm upgrade plan v1.31.4      # target a specific version
```
Typical output sections:
- **Current cluster version** and the latest stable it found.
- A **component table** (kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, kube-proxy, CoreDNS, etcd) showing *current → target*.
- The exact `kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z` command to run.

### The full control-plane upgrade sequence (context)
```bash
# 1. upgrade the kubeadm binary (package manager) to the target version
apt-get install -y kubeadm=1.31.4-*        # or dnf

# 2. read the plan, then apply (control-plane node first)
kubeadm upgrade plan
kubeadm upgrade apply v1.31.4

# 3. drain the node, upgrade kubelet + kubectl packages, restart kubelet
kubectl drain <cp> --ignore-daemonsets
apt-get install -y kubelet=1.31.4-* kubectl=1.31.4-*
systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl uncordon <cp>

# 4. on each worker: upgrade kubeadm, then `kubeadm upgrade node`, then kubelet
kubeadm upgrade node
```
| Command | Role |
|---|---|
| `kubeadm upgrade plan` | read-only report |
| `kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z` | upgrades the **control plane** (run on first CP node) |
| `kubeadm upgrade node` | upgrades **additional CP nodes and workers** |

### Reading the version string
```bash
kubectl version                 # shows Client Version AND Server Version
kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion   # just the server string
kubectl version -o yaml         # YAML form
```
| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `clientVersion.gitVersion` | your local kubectl |
| `serverVersion.gitVersion` | the running kube-apiserver — the "cluster version" |

Writing it to a file on a kind node:
```bash
V=$(kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion)
docker exec "$CP" sh -c "echo $V > /tmp/serverversion.txt"
docker exec "$CP" cat /tmp/serverversion.txt      # v1.31.0
```

### Upgrade rules you must know
- **One minor version per hop** — 1.30 → 1.31 is allowed; 1.30 → 1.32 is not.
- **Control plane before workers.**
- **kubeadm binary first**, then `kubeadm upgrade apply`, then kubelet/kubectl packages.
- kubelet may trail the apiserver by up to **3 minor** versions, never lead it.
- `kubeadm upgrade apply` also **renews all certificates** unless `--certificate-renewal=false`.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`kubeadm upgrade plan` is read-only** — it never changes the cluster. `apply` is the mutating command.
- The **`kubectl version --short` flag was removed** — don't use it; parse plain output or `-o json`.
- Confusing **Client Version** with **Server Version** — the plan and skew rules care about the server (apiserver).
- Can't skip minor versions; the plan will refuse a 2-minor jump.
- On kind, redirects belong **inside** the node: `docker exec "$CP" sh -c 'echo ... > /tmp/f'`.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubeadm upgrade plan                                   # read-only report
kubectl version                                        # Server Version line
kubectl version -o json | jq -r .serverVersion.gitVersion
# then (real upgrade): kubeadm upgrade apply vX.Y.Z
```

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a Pod that won't schedule
questions.teach:
A Pod stuck `Pending` with no node is a scheduling problem. `kubectl describe pod

` Events show the reason — a common one is every candidate node being `unschedulable` (cordoned), so the scheduler has nowhere to place it. **Gotcha:** fix the NODE (uncordon it), not the pod — an already-created Pending pod schedules on its own once a matching node becomes schedulable.
questions.prompt:
Pod `maint-app` in `default` is stuck `Pending` — it is pinned (via nodeSelector) to a worker that is currently cordoned. Diagnose WHY it won't schedule and fix it so it runs. Do NOT delete or recreate the pod, and do NOT edit the pod's nodeSelector.

Target: pod `maint-app` is `Running` AND the worker it targets is schedulable.
questions.hint: `kubectl describe pod maint-app` and `kubectl get nodes` — one worker shows `SchedulingDisabled`. That's $W1. Uncordon it: `kubectl uncordon "$W1"`, then watch `kubectl get pod maint-app -o wide`.
questions.solution:
kubectl describe pod maint-app
kubectl get nodes
# $W1 is cordoned (SchedulingDisabled) and maint-app's nodeSelector pins it there
kubectl uncordon "$W1"
kubectl get pod maint-app -o wide

verification.description: maint-app is Running and its target worker ($W1) is schedulable

questions.eli5:
A pod stuck on `Pending` is like a passenger standing at the airport with a boarding pass but no gate — the plane (node) they're booked on just isn't accepting them. The fix almost never involves the passenger; it's the gate that's the problem.

When a pod won't schedule, the first thing you do is **ask it why**: `kubectl describe pod <name>` and scroll to the **Events** at the bottom. The scheduler leaves a plain-English note there, like *"0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) were unschedulable."* That line is the whole mystery solved.

Here the story is: the pod has a `nodeSelector` that pins it to one specific worker, and that worker has been **cordoned** (someone put up the "no new check-ins" sign — maybe for maintenance, maybe they forgot to take it down). So the only node the pod is allowed on refuses new pods, and it waits.

The fix is to heal the **node**, not the pod: `kubectl uncordon <node>`. The moment a matching schedulable node appears, the scheduler places the already-Pending pod on its own — you don't recreate it.

**Watch out for:**

- **Fix the node, not the pod.** Don't delete or recreate a Pending pod — once a valid node becomes schedulable, it schedules itself.
- **Read the Events.** `kubectl describe pod` tells you the exact reason; don't guess.
- A cordoned node shows `SchedulingDisabled` in `kubectl get nodes` — that's the smoking gun.
- Don't touch the pod's `nodeSelector` here — the selector is correct; the node was simply unavailable.
- Other common Pending causes (for your toolbox): insufficient CPU/memory, an untolerated taint, or a missing node label. The Events line distinguishes them.
questions.deepDive:
## Diagnosing a Pending pod (cordoned-node edition) — full rundown ### Mental model A pod in `Pending` with no assigned node means the **scheduler couldn't find a node that satisfies all its constraints**. The scheduler records *why* in the pod's **Events**. Your job is to read the reason and fix the **environment** (node/labels/taints/resources) — the pod reschedules itself once a suitable node exists. Don't recreate the pod unless its own spec is wrong. ### The diagnosis loop ```bash kubectl get pod

-o wide # STATUS Pending, NODE kubectl describe pod

| sed -n '/Events/,$p' # the scheduler's reason kubectl get nodes # look for SchedulingDisabled / NotReady kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp # cluster-wide context ``` A cordoned-node failure looks like: ``` Warning FailedScheduling default-scheduler 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) were unschedulable, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector. ``` `kubectl get nodes` then shows the target worker as `Ready,SchedulingDisabled`. ### Decode the "0/N nodes are available" message | Message fragment | Root cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | `node(s) were unschedulable` | node **cordoned** (`.spec.unschedulable=true`) | `kubectl uncordon ` | | `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector` | `nodeSelector`/affinity has no matching node | label the node or correct the selector | | `had untolerated taint {k: v}` | node tainted, pod lacks toleration | add toleration or remove taint | | `Insufficient cpu` / `Insufficient memory` | no node has room | free resources / lower requests / add a node | | `node(s) had volume node affinity conflict` | PV is zone-locked away from fit nodes | match zones / use a different PV | | pod `Pending`, **no Events at all** | `nodeName` set to a bad node (scheduler bypassed) | fix `nodeName` (recreate) | ### This scenario: cordoned target node The pod's `nodeSelector` pins it to one worker that is cordoned. The selector is **correct**; the node is simply refusing new pods. Fix the node: ```bash kubectl uncordon "$W1" kubectl get pod maint-app -o wide # flips to Running on $W1 within seconds ``` No pod edit, no delete — a Pending pod is picked up automatically when a matching schedulable node appears. ### Why NOT to touch the pod - Most pod fields (incl. `nodeSelector`, `nodeName`) are **immutable** — you'd have to delete/recreate, which the task forbids and which loses the "it self-heals" lesson. - Recreating masks the real fault (the cordoned node) and it would just go Pending again. ### Gotchas & exam traps - **Fix the node, not the pod.** Uncordon/label/untaint the node; the scheduler does the rest. - **Always read Events first** — the message names the exact constraint. Guessing wastes exam time. - `Ready,SchedulingDisabled` = cordoned; "Ready" alone doesn't mean schedulable. - **No Events + Pending** points to `nodeName` (scheduler was bypassed), a different class of bug. - A forgotten `drain`/`cordon` from maintenance is the usual real-world cause here. - Distinguish `Pending` (not scheduled) from `ContainerCreating` (scheduled, image/volume pulling) — different problem. ### Quick reference ```bash kubectl describe pod maint-app | sed -n '/Events/,$p' # read the reason kubectl get nodes # find SchedulingDisabled kubectl uncordon "$W1" # fix the NODE kubectl get pod maint-app -o wide # -> Running ```
